deep.reconstruction:
This page has no formulas. It is a methodological remark that explains the curvilinear coordinates (p,q) used on the previous page (16r). There, the area integral of (d(f dq/dq)/dp − d(f dq/dp)/dq) dp dq is reduced to a boundary integral, i.e. Green's/Stokes' theorem in coordinates p,q adapted to the surface. The p-curves are closed and the q-curves run from the boundary to an interior max/min point. The style ('wie Sie sehen') suggests explanatory notes addressed to an editor or correspondent. The minimal-surface material was edited posthumously by Hattendorff in 1867.

Content, restated:
(1) The quantities p, q are introduced only so that each point of the surface is determined uniquely (one-to-one). The other variable quantities, such as x, y, z and the functions f, are not required to be expressed explicitly in p, q. They are only thought of as depending on them, i.e. single-valued functions of the point.
(2) Alongside p, q one can, and will, keep a second system of variables in which the other quantities are actually expressed. In modern terms: separate the parametrisation used for integration (a chart or uniformizing parameter) from the coordinates in which formulas are written.
(3) Analogy: for functions of one complex variable, besides the variable z one really needs further quantities that determine the points of the branched covering surface (Riemann surface) uniquely. Over a branch point z alone does not separate the sheets; one needs a local uniformizing parameter. Example (mine): t with z = z0 + t^m near a branch point of order m−1.
(4) For functions of several complex variables, instead of such (Riemann) surfaces, with branching loci in place of branch points, one needs distinguished systems of real variables. That is, real coordinate systems that determine the points of the multi-sheeted domain uniquely. In modern language: charts or local coordinates on a Riemann domain or complex manifold spread over C^n.

No computation is performed. The page justifies the use of the abstract parameters (p,q) in the integral transformation of the previous page.
errors: No mathematical errors; the page contains no derivation.

Unjustified as stated: the existence of 'ausgezeichnete Systeme von reeller Veränderlichen' for several complex variables is only asserted, not shown. In C^n the branch locus has real codimension 2 and local uniformization is in general not possible (singularities of the branch locus). So the remark is programmatic, not a theorem.

results.what: Distinguishing coordinates that merely label points uniquely (p,q) from the variables in which the functions are expressed; integrating in such adapted coordinates.
results.modern_name: Local charts / parametrisation of a manifold; coordinate-independent integration (Green–Stokes in curvilinear coordinates)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1854 Habilitation, manifold concept); formalised by Weyl (1913) for Riemann surfaces

results.what: Points of a branched covering surface over the z-plane need additional quantities beyond z to be determined uniquely.
results.modern_name: Local uniformizing parameter on a Riemann surface

results.what: For several complex variables, the role of the branched Riemann surface is taken over by distinguished systems of real variables that determine points uniquely (branch loci instead of branch points).
results.modern_name: Riemann domains (unramified/ramified domains spread over C^n), real local coordinates on complex analytic spaces
results.usually_credited_to: Weierstrass (analytic continuation in several variables), Thullen (1931–32), H. Cartan, Oka (1930s–50s)

deep.surprise_reason: The ideas behind (1)–(3) are Riemann's well-known philosophy (manifolds, Riemann surfaces, local parameters). The passing remark that several complex variables require a replacement for Riemann surfaces is mildly notable as an early explicit statement. However, it is vague and programmatic, and Riemann's interest in several complex variables (Abelian/theta functions) is known. It is not a result.

checkable.asserts: Illustration (mine): w = sqrt(z) is single-valued in the uniformizing parameter t with z = t**2, which separates the two sheets over the branch point z=0.
Identity behind the previous page's integral transformation: d(f dg/dq)/dp − d(f dg/dp)/dq = Jacobian(f,g)/(p,q), the integrand of ∬ df dg (coordinate-free in p,q).
